## ai-agent-incidents

Page: https://basitalisandhu.github.io/ai-agent-incidents/
Repository: https://github.com/basitalisandhu/ai-agent-incidents
Theme: Data and lists

An open dataset of AI agent and LLM security incidents, with a browsable site.

An open, structured dataset (an incident database) of publicly documented security
incidents, vulnerability disclosures and threat reports involving LLM applications and
AI agents, for security engineers, researchers and policy teams who need evidence about
prompt injection, data exfiltration, supply-chain compromise and agent misuse rather
than headlines. Every event is one schema-validated JSON file, coded under a written codebook by the role AI plays
in it (**weapon**, **target** or **surface**), how the attack got in, what authority the
AI held, how the effect got out, and what harm resulted, and cross-referenced to the
OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications, the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications and
MITRE ATLAS.

Browse it at **https://basitalisandhu.github.io/ai-agent-incidents/** (searchable
table, one page per event, [RSS feed](https://basitalisandhu.github.io/ai-agent-incidents/feed.xml),
[JSON](https://basitalisandhu.github.io/ai-agent-incidents/incidents.json),
[CSV](https://basitalisandhu.github.io/ai-agent-incidents/incidents.csv),
[stats](https://basitalisandhu.github.io/ai-agent-incidents/stats.json)).

Latest release: v1.0.0 (2026-10-13) https://github.com/basitalisandhu/ai-agent-incidents/releases/tag/v1.0.0

## agent-skills-state-2026

Page: https://basitalisandhu.github.io/agent-skills-state-2026/
Repository: https://github.com/basitalisandhu/agent-skills-state-2026
Theme: Data and lists

Monthly study of public agent skill, plugin and MCP repositories: dataset, method, hand-checked precision and scripts.

*Muhammad Basit Ali, 13 October 2026. Dataset, method and scripts are in this repository. Data and text: CC BY 4.0. Code: MIT.*

*This is the first edition. The scan is re-run every month and each month's data is added alongside; see [Updated monthly](https://github.com/basitalisandhu/agent-skills-state-2026#updated-monthly).*

Agent skills, plugin marketplaces and MCP servers are now installed the way browser extensions once were: someone finds a repository, copies a line into a config file and the agent gains new instructions, new shell access or a new process that starts with every session. We wanted to know what that supply looks like on the ground, measured rather than guessed. So we took a random sample of 2,999 public GitHub repositories that ship a `SKILL.md`, a plugin or marketplace manifest, or an MCP `server.json`, scanned them with open-source tools, and hand-checked the scanners before trusting them.

Latest release: v1.0.0 (2026-10-13) https://github.com/basitalisandhu/agent-skills-state-2026/releases/tag/v1.0.0

## awesome-agent-security

Page: https://basitalisandhu.github.io/awesome-agent-security/
Repository: https://github.com/basitalisandhu/awesome-agent-security
Theme: Data and lists

Curated list of AI agent security tools, papers and datasets.

> Curated list of AI agent security tools, papers and datasets: runtime controls, sandboxes, scanners for MCP servers and skills, static analysis, red teaming, incident records, threat models and standards.

An AI agent is a model that can read untrusted content and call tools with real privileges. Securing one means controlling what it may touch, isolating what it runs, scanning what it loads, and measuring how it fails. Every entry below exists on GitHub and is maintained; descriptions are the projects' own words, shortened. Maintained by [Muhammad Basit Ali](https://github.com/basitalisandhu); projects by the maintainer are listed in their sections like any other entry. See [contributing.md](https://github.com/basitalisandhu/awesome-agent-security/blob/main/contributing.md) for the inclusion criteria and [SECURITY.md](https://github.com/basitalisandhu/awesome-agent-security/blob/main/SECURITY.md) to report a listed project that has turned malicious.

## Post: What the OWASP Agentic Top 10 maps to in 88 real incidents

URL: https://basitalisandhu.github.io/posts/what-the-owasp-agentic-top-10-maps-to-in-88-real-incidents/
Date: 2026-10-16

When a team asks me which agent risks to plan for, the [OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications for 2026](https://genai.owasp.org/resource/owasp-top-10-for-agentic-applications-for-2026/) is the list I point them to first. It is a good list. But a list of categories does not tell you which ones you will actually meet, what they look like on the ground, or what sits outside the list altogether.

So I counted. The [ai-agent-incidents](https://github.com/basitalisandhu/ai-agent-incidents) dataset I maintain has 88 publicly documented events from February 2023 to September 2026: 29 incidents, 48 vulnerability disclosures and 11 threat reports. Each one is coded from its primary source under a [written codebook](https://github.com/basitalisandhu/ai-agent-incidents/blob/main/docs/codebook.md), and each carries a mapping to the ten `ASI` categories where the source supports one. This week I added a script that cross-tabulates those mappings against the other coded fields. Every number below comes from it.

## How to reproduce the numbers

The script is standard-library Python, reads the committed JSON records and needs no network:

```console
$ git clone https://github.com/basitalisandhu/ai-agent-incidents
$ cd ai-agent-incidents
$ python3 scripts/agentic_crosstab.py --stdout
## Coverage

- Events: **88** (2023-02 to 2026-09)
- Mapped to at least one ASI category: **57** (64.8%)
- Mapped to none: **31** (35.2%)
- Mapped events with two or more categories: **26** of 57 (45.6%)

| lens | events | mapped | unmapped | mapped share |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `surface` | 51 | 46 | 5 | 90.2% |
| `target` | 21 | 7 | 14 | 33.3% |
| `weapon` | 16 | 4 | 12 | 25.0% |
...
```

The full output is committed as [docs/owasp-agentic-crosstab.md](https://github.com/basitalisandhu/ai-agent-incidents/blob/main/docs/owasp-agentic-crosstab.md), and a test fails if it drifts from the records. The per-category counts across the ten categories are: ASI01 Agent Goal Hijack 26, ASI05 Unexpected Code Execution 17, ASI02 Tool Misuse and Exploitation 16, ASI04 Agentic Supply Chain Vulnerabilities 12, ASI03 Identity and Privilege Abuse 7, ASI10 Rogue Agents 5, ASI06 Memory and Context Poisoning 4, ASI07 Insecure Inter-Agent Communication 1, and ASI08 Cascading Agent Failures and ASI09 Human-Agent Trust Exploitation none.

## Six things the cross-tab shows

**1. The list covers AI as an attack surface, and not much else.** The dataset codes every event by the role AI plays: a *surface* (the agent is a path to someone else's assets), a *target* (the AI's own data, prompts, keys or serving stack are attacked) or a *weapon* (an attacker uses AI against people or systems). 46 of the 51 surface events (90.2%) map to at least one ASI category. Only 7 of 21 target events and 4 of 16 weapon events do. Of the 31 events that map to nothing, 26 are target or weapon events: exposed databases behind AI products, leaked API tokens, attacks on model-serving software, deepfake fraud and AI-orchestrated intrusion campaigns.

That is not a flaw in the list. It says what it is for. If your threat model only uses the Agentic Top 10, it will cover the agent you build and miss the stack it runs on and the attackers who now use the same tools. 85 of the 88 events map to at least one of the three frameworks the dataset uses (the OWASP LLM Top 10 and MITRE ATLAS are the other two), so use them together.

**2. Goal hijack is the front door, and it comes in through content.** ASI01 is the largest category at 26 events, and 25 of those 26 are coded as indirect prompt injection. The content arrived through a web page in 9, a document in 6, a repository issue or pull request in 4, and email and support tickets in 2 each. Nobody typed the attack into the chat box; the agent read it while doing its job.

**3. "Read-only" did not keep data in.** 12 of the 26 goal hijack events involve an agent coded with read-only authority. In 10 of those 12 the outcome was data exfiltration, and in 9 the data left through an image or link fetch: the agent was told to render a URL with the data in its query string, and the client fetched it. If your approval for an agent rests on "it can only read", ask what it can render and what it can fetch.

**4. Categories travel together.** 26 of the 57 mapped events (45.6%) carry two or more categories. The common pairs are ASI01 with ASI02 (9 events) and ASI01 with ASI05 (6). In practice goal hijack is the start of the chain and tool misuse or code execution is where the harm happens. I find it more useful to put controls at the consequence end, on what a hijacked agent can call and run, than to rely on spotting every injection.

**5. Unexpected code execution means a shell.** All 17 ASI05 events involve an agent coded with shell or code execution authority, and 16 ended in code execution. Across the whole dataset, 38 of 88 events involve that authority, more than any other. A coding agent with a terminal is the single most represented kind of agent in the public record.

**6. Identity abuse is under-reported, not rare.** ASI03 has only 7 events, though 5 events involve an agent holding cloud credentials and 5 involve repository write access. Only one of the cloud-credential events and one of the repository-write events is mapped to ASI03. My reading is that public write-ups describe the injection and the payload, and rarely the identity the agent ran as or how broad its grants were, so the mapping cannot be made with confidence. The blast radius was still set by those grants. I wrote about that gap in [Agent identities are the new service accounts](/posts/agent-identities-are-the-new-service-accounts/), and [agent-off-switch](/agent-off-switch/) is the tool I use to list and stop those identities.

## The empty columns

Two categories have no events at all, and a third has one. ASI08 Cascading Agent Failures and ASI09 Human-Agent Trust Exploitation are at zero, and ASI07 Insecure Inter-Agent Communication at one.

An empty column in a sample of public reports is not evidence that a risk is rare. 48 of the 88 events are vulnerability disclosures, and a disclosure usually describes one bug in one product with a clean proof of concept. A failure that cascades across several agents, or an agent that talks a human approver into clicking yes, is harder to show in one advisory and harder to attribute in an incident report. These may be the categories most likely to be under-counted rather than the least likely to happen.

ASI10 Rogue Agents is the opposite case. Its 5 events are all incidents, not disclosures, and 4 of them are coded as autonomous operations: evaluation and research agents that went outside their intended scope, breached systems they were not meant to touch or published data they should not have. These are recent: the year table shows how mapping coverage moved from 4 of 11 events in 2023 and 5 of 13 in 2024 to 24 of 32 in both 2025 and 2026, as agents with real tools became the subject of most reports.

## What I take from it for a threat model

For an agent I am reviewing, the counts suggest an order of work:

1. **Treat every input the agent reads as untrusted**, not just chat. Web pages, documents, issues, pull requests, tickets and email are where ASI01 came in.
2. **Control egress, including link and image rendering.** That one channel carried 9 of the 26 hijack events out.
3. **Constrain what a hijacked agent can call and run.** Tool allowlists, scoped shell access and sandboxing address ASI02 and ASI05, the categories that most often follow ASI01.
4. **Size the identity before the pilot starts.** The record will not tell you how often ASI03 happens, because write-ups rarely describe the grants. Assume it applies.
5. **Pin what the agent loads.** ASI04 events came in through packages in 7 of 12 cases. My [study of 2,999 public skill and MCP repositories](/posts/the-state-of-public-agent-skills-and-mcp-servers/) found 46.0% of repositories that configure a local MCP server start at least one with no pinned version, and [skill-scan-gate](/skill-scan-gate/) fails a pull request that adds one.
6. **Then add the target and weapon lenses**, with the OWASP LLM Top 10, MITRE ATLAS and ordinary application security.

[agent-threat-model](/agent-threat-model/) turns a YAML description of the agent into a ranked threat register and control checklist, offline and in CI, and every threat it reports carries its OWASP Agentic, OWASP LLM and ATLAS ids.

## What the data cannot tell you

- **It is a convenience sample.** It holds what vendors, researchers and journalists chose to publish. No share in this post estimates how common anything is in the world; it describes 88 records.
- **The mappings are one maintainer's reading.** Lens and vector were blind-coded twice for the paper behind the seed data (kappa 0.82 and 0.87 with the second coder). The OWASP mappings were not, and an empty mapping means "no confident mapping", not "none applies".
- **Dates are the month of the public report**, not of the event.
- **Small cells are small.** ASI06, ASI07 and ASI10 rest on one to five events each; read them as examples, not trends.

Each record links its primary source, so any count here can be checked against the events behind it. Corrections and new events are welcome as [issues or pull requests](https://github.com/basitalisandhu/ai-agent-incidents/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md); a new event needs a public primary source.

## Post: The state of public agent skills and MCP servers

URL: https://basitalisandhu.github.io/posts/the-state-of-public-agent-skills-and-mcp-servers/
Date: 2026-10-13

Agent skills, plugin marketplaces and MCP servers are now installed the way browser extensions once were. Someone finds a repository, copies a line into a config file, and the agent gains new instructions, new shell access or a new process that starts with every session. I wanted to know what that supply looks like on the ground, measured rather than guessed.

So on 13 October 2026 I took a random sample of 2,999 public GitHub repositories that ship a `SKILL.md`, a plugin or marketplace manifest, or an MCP `server.json`. I fetched only the agent configuration files, ran nothing, scanned them with open-source tools and checked the scanners by hand before trusting any number. The dataset, method, scripts and charts are in [agent-skills-state-2026](https://github.com/basitalisandhu/agent-skills-state-2026), with the data under CC BY 4.0.

## What the sample is

The repositories came from GitHub code search: 31 queries split by file size, which surfaced 7,456 distinct non-fork repositories. I drew 3,000 at random and one failed to download. The result is young and mostly small: 2,512 of the 2,999 were created in 2026 and the median repository has 4 stars, though 434 have 100 or more. 2,621 contain at least one skill, 336,285 `SKILL.md` files in all. 373 have an agent hook configuration and 346 configure at least one MCP server that runs as a local process.

Every share below has its own denominator, because a pinning finding only makes sense for repositories that configure an MCP server, and a skill finding only for repositories with skills.

## Five findings

**1. Most repositories give no way to report a vulnerability.** 2,459 of 2,999 (82.0%) have no `SECURITY.md`. Popularity barely helps: among the 434 repositories with 100 or more stars it is still 75.6%. If you find a problem in a skill you depend on, there is usually no stated route to tell the author privately.

**2. Nearly half of MCP configurations run code that can change under you.** Of the 346 repositories that configure a local MCP server, 159 (46.0%) start at least one with no pinned version. 100 (28.9%) run an npm package through `npx` with no exact version, 63 (18.2%) ask for the `latest` tag outright, and 38 (11.0%) run a Python package without a version. Each session start can fetch whatever the package owner, or anyone who takes over the package, published last. The 100-plus star band is the worst for this, at 57.8%, though on only 45 repositories.

**3. A third ship with no licence.** 982 of 2,999 (32.7%) have no licence file at the root. For zero-star repositories it is 53.7% (of 984); for repositories with 100 or more stars, 16.6% (of 434). Without a licence, a team has no clear right to copy a skill into its own repository, which is how most skills end up being used.

**4. One in six skill repositories gives a skill the whole shell.** 407 of the 2,621 repositories with skills (15.5%) declare at least one skill whose `allowed-tools` grants `Bash` with no command scoping, 10,073 declarations in total. That is not proof of misuse. It does remove the host's chance to ask before each command.

**5. One in eight skill repositories has a skill whose header does not parse.** In 330 of 2,621 (12.6%) at least one `SKILL.md` has YAML front matter that a standard parser rejects, usually because a description contains an unquoted colon. That is 4,761 of 336,285 files (1.4%). A host that cannot read a skill's name and description cannot decide when to load it, and nothing tells the author.

Two smaller results. Of the 373 repositories with hook configurations, 13 have a hook that by default calls a host other than the local machine; I read every flagged hook by hand to get that number. And 146 of 2,621 skill repositories have a description over 1,024 characters, a common host limit.

## How far to trust the scanners

I did not report a measure until I had checked how often it was right. Unrestricted Bash was right in 10 of 10 sampled findings, unpinned MCP servers in 19 of 22, and YAML failures in 10 of 10. The licence and security-policy checks agreed with GitHub's own detection for 99% and 98% of findings.

Some measures did not survive. The linter's "no Use when sentence" check was right only 5 times in 12, because most descriptions it flagged did say when to use the skill, in other words or another language, so I dropped it. The secret rules were the weakest of all: a check for provider tokens was right 0 times in 10, mostly because the hits were scanner regexes, placeholders and example responses in documentation.

That matters for anyone counting "leaked secrets" in public skill repositories. The secret-shaped-string rules fired in 471 of the 2,999. After triaging every hit by structure, without displaying any value, 30 possible live credentials in 17 repositories remained. Before publishing, I re-checked each one: 4 were test values or shortened examples, and the owners of the other 13 were notified, by email where an address existed and otherwise with a short public notice that names no file or key type, since none had private vulnerability reporting enabled.

## What to do before installing a skill or MCP server

- **Pin every MCP server.** Write `package@1.2.3`, never a bare name or `@latest`, and update on purpose. It is the most common finding that can run new code without review, and it is a one-line fix.
- **Read `allowed-tools`.** A skill that asks for unscoped `Bash` should say why, or be scoped to the commands it needs.
- **Read the hook scripts, not only the manifest.** Hooks run on every tool call. Most I read stay local, but some phone home on install or post session data to a webhook.
- **Check the licence before copying a skill** into your own repository.
- **Lint your own skills in CI.** A colon in a description is enough to stop a host reading the header, and it is cheap to catch.
- **Treat a scanner's secret count as a reading list,** not a result.
- **Give the agent its own identity and know how to switch it off.** Pinning and scoping limit what a skill can do; the identity it runs as limits the damage when one goes wrong. I wrote about that in [Agent identities are the new service accounts](/posts/agent-identities-are-the-new-service-accounts/).

## What the data does not show

It does not show that any repository is malicious or that any finding was exploited. It measures the presence of patterns at one commit on the default branch, statically, without running a skill, a hook or a server. It describes what GitHub code search surfaces, which leans towards young, small, personal projects; a curated marketplace may look better. Some precision samples are small, between 5 and 12 findings, and none of them say anything about what the scanners miss. "Fails YAML parsing" means one strict parser rejects it; an agent host may be more lenient.

It is also a snapshot. Search results change daily, so a rerun of the scripts draws a different sample. The method is what reproduces, and the repository has everything needed to run it again.

## The data

The repository [basitalisandhu/agent-skills-state-2026](https://github.com/basitalisandhu/agent-skills-state-2026) has one row per repository in CSV and JSON, the precision table, the chart data, the full method and the scripts, with a citation file if you want to reference it. Corrections are welcome as issues.

## Post: Agent identities are the new service accounts

URL: https://basitalisandhu.github.io/posts/agent-identities-are-the-new-service-accounts/
Date: 2026-10-13

Part of my job is running access reviews. Human accounts are the easy part: there is an HR system, a manager, a leaver process. The hard part has always been the service accounts, and AI agents have made that part bigger.

An agent does not act with its own authority. It acts with whatever identity it was given. In practice that is an Entra app registration or service principal, a managed identity, an AWS IAM role or an access key, a GitHub App installation or a deploy key. These are the service accounts we already struggle to govern, and agents add more of them, created faster, often by a team running a pilot rather than by the people who run identity.

The pattern I keep seeing has three parts. Nobody owns the list. Nobody recertifies it. And when something goes wrong, nobody can stop one of these identities quickly and prove it is stopped.

## Why this is an identity problem, not a model problem

The [OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications for 2026](https://genai.owasp.org/resource/owasp-top-10-for-agentic-applications-for-2026/) lists ASI03, Identity & Privilege Abuse, as its own category. The [OWASP announcement](https://genai.owasp.org/2025/12/09/owasp-top-10-for-agentic-applications-the-benchmark-for-agentic-security-in-the-age-of-autonomous-ai/) describes leaked credentials letting agents operate "far beyond their intended scope". Whatever an agent is tricked into doing, the blast radius is set by its identity's grants.

Microsoft says much the same in its [governance guidance for agent identities](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/id-governance/agent-id-governance-overview): agents have historically reached Microsoft services through tools that use service principals. [Microsoft Entra Agent ID](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/agent-id/what-is-microsoft-entra-agent-id) is its answer, a dedicated identity type for agents built from agent identity blueprints, with Conditional Access, Identity Protection, governance and audit logs extended to them. It is a good direction. It does not cover the AWS role your coding agent assumes or the GitHub App it pushes with, and many agents in Entra still run as ordinary app registrations.

## The failure modes I look for

These are the patterns I look for first in a review.

- **An ownerless identity with a tenant-wide Graph application permission.** An application permission such as `Mail.ReadWrite` works for every mailbox in the tenant with no signed-in user. If nobody owns the app registration, nobody will notice when it is misused, and nobody will answer the question "do we still need this?".
- **A role with `Action: "*"` that a CI agent assumes through OIDC.** Federation is the right way to give a pipeline credentials. But an OIDC trust to a role with `*` on `*` means any workflow that can satisfy the trust condition has the whole account.
- **A credential older than 90 days.** A client secret or access key that has not been rotated is a long-lived secret sitting in a pipeline variable, a vault or a laptop. AWS's [IAM security best practices](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/best-practices.html) say to require workloads to use temporary credentials with IAM roles, and to update access keys where long-term credentials cannot be avoided.
- **An owner who left.** The identity had an owner when it was created. That person moved on, the owner field was cleared or now points at a disabled account, and the identity kept working.
- **A GitHub App with administration write on every repository.** Administration covers settings, branch protection and deletion. GitHub's [best practices for creating a GitHub App](https://docs.github.com/en/apps/creating-github-apps/about-creating-github-apps/best-practices-for-creating-a-github-app) start with selecting the minimum permissions the app needs. Read-write deploy keys are a smaller version of the same problem: GitHub's [deploy key documentation](https://docs.github.com/en/authentication/connecting-to-github-with-ssh/managing-deploy-keys) notes that they have no expiry date and are tied to the repository, not to a user.
- **Stopping a role does not end existing sessions.** Changing an IAM role's trust policy stops new sessions. Credentials already issued stay valid until they expire. AWS documents how to [revoke role sessions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_roles_use_revoke-sessions.html) with an `AWSRevokeOlderSessions` policy keyed on `aws:TokenIssueTime`. If your off switch is "edit the trust policy", it is half a switch.

## The controls

None of these controls is new. They are the service account controls, applied to a population that grew while nobody was counting.

1. **Inventory.** One list of every non-human identity across Microsoft 365, AWS and GitHub, with the likely agents marked.
2. **Owner.** A named person or team for each one. No owner, no access.
3. **Least privilege.** Grants sized to the task, not to the pilot. AWS points to IAM Access Analyzer to generate policies from access activity, and GitHub to minimum permissions and limiting the repositories an app can reach.
4. **Credential hygiene.** No secrets where a federated or managed credential will do; rotation and an age limit where a secret is unavoidable; expired credentials deleted.
5. **Recertification.** On a schedule, the owner confirms the identity is still needed and its grants are still right. AWS's best practices include regularly reviewing and removing unused users, roles, permissions and credentials.
6. **An off switch.** A tested, ordered procedure to stop one identity: disable it, end live sessions, remove grants and credentials, and check the audit log.
7. **Drift in CI.** New identities, new grants and lost owners between reviews should fail a check until a person accepts them.

## How agent-off-switch maps to those controls

I built [agent-off-switch](https://github.com/basitalisandhu/agent-off-switch) (`aos`) for the reviews I run. It reads saved exports from Entra, AWS and GitHub, plus an optional `agents.csv` register, and works offline with no credentials of its own. Everything below is real output from the synthetic demo tenant that ships in the repository: the ids are fake and the AWS account is the documentation account `111122223333`.

**Inventory, owner, least privilege and credential hygiene** come from `aos review`, which ranks findings by blast radius (0 to 100) and gives each a fix:

```console
$ aos review examples/demo-tenant --as-of 2026-10-09
# Agent access review

As of 2026-10-09: 13 non-human identities, 11 look like agents. 15 findings (8 error), ranked by blast radius (0 to 100, see docs/scoring.md).

## 4 agent identities nobody owns

- **coding-agent-runner** `aws-role:coding-agent-runner` (blast radius 100): Action * on Resource *
  - switch off: `aos off examples/demo-tenant aws-role:coding-agent-runner`
- **repo-autopilot** `github-app:repo-autopilot` (blast radius 95): administration: write on every repository (settings, branch protection, deletion)
  - switch off: `aos off examples/demo-tenant github-app:repo-autopilot`
- **mail-triage-agent** `entra:aaaaaaaa-0000-4000-8000-000000000001` (blast radius 90): Mail.ReadWrite as an application permission changes data for every user in the tenant
  - switch off: `aos off examples/demo-tenant entra:aaaaaaaa-0000-4000-8000-000000000001`
...
```

The findings table that follows covers the rest of the failure modes above, including a client secret 434 days old and a deploy key that can push, each with its fix.

The same review can be written as SARIF for GitHub code scanning. `aos inventory` gives the full table of identities with owners, credentials, grants and last use, as Markdown, CSV or JSON.

**The off switch** is `aos off`. It prints an ordered runbook and runs nothing. For the coding agent's role, the first two steps are the point I made above: stop new sessions, then revoke the ones already issued.

```console
$ aos off examples/demo-tenant aws-role:coding-agent-runner --as-of 2026-10-09
# Off-switch runbook: coding-agent-runner

Identity `aws-role:coding-agent-runner` (aws-iam-role on aws). Owners: none recorded. Blast radius 100. Exports as of 2026-10-09.

aos printed these commands and ran none of them. Run each change in order, then its verification, and keep the verification output for the incident record. Values in <angle brackets> are for you to fill in.

## 1 disable

### Step 1: Stop new sessions: replace the trust policy (now trusts Federated: arn:aws:iam::111122223333:oidc-provider/token.actions.githubusercontent.com) with a deny-all one; save the current one first
...
## 2 revoke sessions and grants

### Step 2: Revoke every session issued before the disable time (the console's Revoke active sessions)
...
## 5 verify with the audit log

### Step 5: Confirm in CloudTrail that nothing succeeded after the disable time
...
## Coverage

Every credential and grant in the exports is named by a step.
```

Each step in the full output has a change command, a verification command and a line to record the time and the person. The coverage line matters: if a grant in the exports is not named by any step, `aos` says so and exits 1.

**Drift in CI** is `aos drift`, which compares a saved inventory with today's exports:

```console
$ aos drift examples/drift/baseline.json examples/demo-tenant --as-of 2026-10-09 --accept examples/drift/accepted.txt
# Agent identity drift

From 2026-09-01 (11 identities) to 2026-10-09 (13 identities): 4 changes, 3 not reviewed.

| Change | Identity | Detail | Reviewed |
|---|---|---|---|
| new-identity | `github-app:repo-autopilot` | repo-autopilot (github-app, no owner, blast radius 95) | **no** |
| new-identity | `github-app:docs-preview-bot` | docs-preview-bot (github-app, web-team@example.com, blast radius 55) | yes |
| new-grant | `aws-role:coding-agent-runner` | agent-all (score 100) | **no** |
| owner-lost | `entra:aaaaaaaa-0000-4000-8000-000000000001` | was owned by messaging-team@example.com; now no owner | **no** |
...
```

It exits 1 while anything is unreviewed, so it can gate a pull request. Accepting a change means adding its key to the accept file, so the decision sits in version control next to the inventory.

## What it does not do

I would rather say this plainly.

- **Recertification is supported, not performed.** `aos` gives you the data a recertification needs: owners, grants, credential ages, last use, and the unused and no-owner findings. It does not send attestations, collect decisions or remove access when nobody answers. That is still a process you run, or a governance product's job.
- **It never changes anything.** It calls no cloud API and runs no command. `off` prints commands for a person to run.
- **It is not real time.** It sees what the exports saw. An identity created after the export is invisible until the next run.
- **It does not read every limit on access.** Azure role assignments, AWS permission boundaries, service control policies, resource policies, Exchange RBAC for Applications scopes and Conditional Access are not read, so a score can overstate reach that one of those limits.
- **An owner who left is only partly covered.** `drift` flags an owner that disappears between two inventories. It does not check whether a named owner's account is still active.
- **It does not judge GitHub App activity** (the installations export has no last-use date) **or look inside agents**: prompts, tool calls and memory are out of scope.
- **It does not replace Entra Agent ID**, an identity governance product or a cloud security platform. It gives you one offline list across platforms and a way to act on it.

## Where to start

If you run access reviews, add the agent identities to the next one. Take the read-only exports, list what exists, and put a name against every row. The ones nobody claims are your first off-switch drill.

The repository is at [github.com/basitalisandhu/agent-off-switch](https://github.com/basitalisandhu/agent-off-switch), with the demo tenant, the [threat model](https://github.com/basitalisandhu/agent-off-switch/blob/main/docs/threat-model.md) and the [scoring rules](https://github.com/basitalisandhu/agent-off-switch/blob/main/docs/scoring.md). Issues and pull requests are welcome, especially new export formats and corrections to the scoring.

## Post: Four open repositories for securing AI agents, and what each is for

URL: https://basitalisandhu.github.io/posts/four-open-repositories-for-securing-ai-agents/
Date: 2026-10-04

Teams are putting language models in front of tools, data and credentials faster than they are writing down what could go wrong. I have spent the year building small, open tools for that gap and for the cloud accounts the agents run in. This post is the map: what each repository is for, where it stops, and the order I would use them in.

None of it is a platform. Each repository stands alone, links its siblings, and does one job. The [project list on this site](/#projects) and the profile at [github.com/basitalisandhu](https://github.com/basitalisandhu) are the index.

## 1. Start from evidence: ai-agent-incidents

Arguments about agent risk are usually made from a handful of famous cases. [ai-agent-incidents](https://github.com/basitalisandhu/ai-agent-incidents) (browse it at [its own site](https://basitalisandhu.github.io/ai-agent-incidents/)) is a structured dataset of publicly documented AI agent and LLM security incidents from February 2023 onwards, one record per event.

Each record was coded from a primary source under a written codebook: the role AI played (weapon, target or surface), the vector, the input channel, the authority the agent held, the output channel and the outcome. Each is mapped to the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications, the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications and MITRE ATLAS. There are JSON and CSV downloads, an RSS feed and a searchable site. The data is CC BY 4.0.

Its limit matters as much as its content. It is a convenience sample of what vendors and researchers chose to disclose, so it over-represents some kinds of incident, and no percentage computed from it estimates how common anything is. An empty mapping means no confident mapping, not that no category applies. If you disagree with a coding, the codebook is in the repository and a pull request is welcome.

## 2. Check the code: agentic-semgrep-rules

Some agent vulnerabilities come down to one short function: model output reaching a shell, a query, a URL fetch or `eval`. [agentic-semgrep-rules](/agentic-semgrep-rules/) is a set of Semgrep rules for AI agent code in Python, TypeScript and JavaScript. They look for model output reaching exec, shells, SQL, URLs, files and HTML, user input in system prompts, over-broad tools, MCP servers without authentication, leaked keys and unsafe model loading, and each rule maps to a CWE and the OWASP lists.

Every rule has tests, so a change to a rule shows up as a failing test rather than a surprise in someone else's pipeline. Tests show what a rule flags; they do not show what it misses. A clean run is one signal, not a clearance, and a false positive is a bug worth reporting.

## 3. Model the system: agent-threat-model

Code scanning finds lines. It does not tell you what an agent can reach if it is tricked. [agent-threat-model](/agent-threat-model/) takes a YAML description of the system (the model, its tools, where its inputs come from, what credentials it holds, who approves what) and produces a ranked threat register under STRIDE and the OWASP Agentic Top 10, a Mermaid diagram, a control checklist, a residual risk score and SARIF for GitHub code scanning.

It runs offline, as a CLI or a GitHub Action, with no model in the loop, so the same description always produces the same output and you can diff a threat model between two pull requests. It only knows what you tell it; the YAML is as good as your description of the system.

## 4. Bring it into the editor and the account: the skill packs

The same habits are packaged as Claude Code skills, each with tested scripts that run offline on saved output rather than on a live system:

- [agent-security-skills](/agent-security-skills/): threat modelling, configuration audits, prompt injection review, MCP server review and incident lookup for securing LLM agents.
- [aws-security-skills](/aws-security-skills/): a read-only AWS account audit, SCP guardrails, IAM least-privilege review and Security Hub and GuardDuty triage.
- [repo-engineering-skills](/repo-engineering-skills/): README and documentation claims checked against the code, audits where every finding cites a resolvable `path:line`.
- [m365-governance-skills](/m365-governance-skills/): Graph permission preflight, Entra ID posture review, Intune baseline check and a quarterly access review pack, from read-only exports.

## How I would use them together

1. Read a few records from the dataset that look like your architecture.
2. Describe your agent in YAML and run the threat-model CLI; compare its register against those records.
3. Run the Semgrep rules over the agent's code, and fix or consciously accept each finding.
4. Put the threat model and the rules in CI so they are still true next quarter.

## What is not here

These tools do not stop an agent from doing anything at runtime. They help you find, describe and review risk before it ships. I would rather say that plainly than imply more.

## What is next

One repository a week. The Show HN sequence runs through the incident dataset, the Semgrep rules and the threat-model CLI; the skill packs and the other developer tooling follow. If you run agents against real systems, I would like to hear what these tools miss. Issues and pull requests are open on every repository, and [the project list](/#projects) has them all.

## Post: Every Claude Code skill I maintain, in one repository

URL: https://basitalisandhu.github.io/posts/every-claude-code-skill-in-one-repository/
Date: 2026-10-04

I keep my Claude Code skills in eight repositories, grouped by job: agent security, AWS, Microsoft 365, compliance evidence, GitHub management, repository engineering, Mac maintenance and everyday development. That split makes sense to maintain. It is awkward to install. This post explains the new repository that puts them together, what is in it, and where it stops.

## Why one repository

Each source repository is its own plugin marketplace. To get everything, you ran `/plugin marketplace add` eight times and `/plugin install` thirteen times, once per plugin. I wanted one clone and one command, and I expect anyone trying more than one pack does too.

So [claude-skills](https://github.com/basitalisandhu/claude-skills) holds all of them: 87 skills in 13 plugins, vendored from the eight source repositories. It is one marketplace, one folder of skills and one install script. The [catalog site](https://basitalisandhu.github.io/claude-skills/) has one page per skill, so you can read what a skill does before you install anything.

The source repositories have not moved. They are still where the skills are written, tested and fixed. The new repository is a copy that stays in step with them.

## What is in it

**Agent security.** [agent-security-skills](/agent-security-skills/) has 8 skills for teams building LLM agents. `agent-threat-model` writes a system description of an agent codebase in a YAML format. `prompt-injection-review` traces untrusted inputs such as web pages, emails and tool results to the tool calls they can reach. `mcp-server-review` is a checklist review of an MCP server implementation.

**AWS security.** [aws-security-skills](/aws-security-skills/) has 9 skills. `aws-account-audit` collects inventory with read-only `aws` commands into a local folder, then evaluates it offline. `scp-guardrails` builds and lints service control policies from a short spec. `security-hub-triage` works through exported Security Hub and GuardDuty findings offline.

**Everyday development.** [claude-dev-skills](/claude-dev-skills/) is the largest source: 40 skills in six plugins called code-quality, data, debugging, devops, docs and security-basics. A few examples: `dead-code-finder` finds probably-unused functions and confirms each candidate before reporting it, `flaky-test-hunter` compares JUnit XML reports from several runs, and `dockerfile-hardening` lints a Dockerfile for images that run as root or use unpinned bases.

**Compliance evidence.** [compliance-evidence-skills](/compliance-evidence-skills/) has 5 skills for ISO 27001 and SOC 2 work. `evidence-pack-builder` turns a folder of GitHub, AWS and Microsoft 365 exports into an integrity-checked evidence pack. `control-map-from-exports` maps those exports to control identifiers. `auditor-narrative-drafter` drafts control narratives with an evidence citation on every claim.

**GitHub management.** [github-manager-skills](/github-manager-skills/) has 3 skills for engineering managers, all computed from saved `gh` exports. `pr-queue-digest` flags pull requests that have waited on review too long. `iteration-report` lists what shipped in a sprint.

**Microsoft 365 governance.** [m365-governance-skills](/m365-governance-skills/) has 9 skills that work from read-only Graph exports. `graph-permission-preflight` checks the permissions an app or connector asks for before anyone consents. `conditional-access-gap-analysis` finds gaps and exclusion problems in Conditional Access. `access-review-pack` builds a quarterly access review package.

**Mac maintenance.** [mac-maintenance-skills](/mac-maintenance-skills/) has 3 skills. `mac-cleanup` starts with a read-only survey of what takes space and memory. `mac-app-leftovers` finds what uninstalled apps left behind.

**Repository engineering.** [repo-engineering-skills](/repo-engineering-skills/) has 10 skills. `docs-truth-check` checks that a README and docs still match the code. `cited-codebase-audit` runs an audit in which every finding cites a `path:line` you can open. `adr-miner` recovers architecture decisions from git history that nobody wrote down.

## How to install

Inside Claude Code, add the marketplace once and install the plugins you want:

```
/plugin marketplace add basitalisandhu/claude-skills
/plugin install aws-security@claude-skills
```

Swap `aws-security` for any of the 13 plugin names. The catalog site lists them.

If you would rather copy the skill folders yourself, clone the repository and run the installer:

```
git clone https://github.com/basitalisandhu/claude-skills
cd claude-skills
python3 install.py --user
```

`--user` copies every skill into `~/.claude/skills`. `--project` puts them in the current project's `.claude/skills` instead. `--only <plugin>` narrows the copy to one plugin, and `--list` prints the catalog without copying anything. The script uses the Python standard library and has no dependencies.

## How it stays honest

A copy is only useful if it matches the original. A workflow runs daily, pulls each source repository and opens a pull request when anything has changed. Nothing lands without that pull request, so every update has a diff you can read.

`SOURCES.json` records where each skill came from: the source repository and the commit it was copied at. If a skill looks different from what you expected, that file tells you which upstream version you have.

The tests live in the source repositories, not here. This repository copies skills; it does not test them again. If you find a bug, please open the issue on the source repository named in `SOURCES.json`. A fix made there reaches this repository through the next sync pull request. A fix made only here would be overwritten by it.

## What it does not do

The skills run offline, on saved exports or on your working tree. The bundled scripts are standard-library Python, make no network calls and send no telemetry. Where a skill needs live data, such as the AWS audit, it tells you which read-only commands to run and then works on the saved output.

Having everything in one place does not change what each skill is. Every `SKILL.md` says what the skill does not do, and you should read that before you rely on a result. A clean report from `secrets-hygiene` or `iam-least-privilege-review` is one signal, not a clearance.

One practical point. Two packs both had a skill called `test-gap-finder`: one in code-quality, which maps source modules to test files, and one in repo-engineering, which finds public functions and entry points no test mentions. They do different things, and skill names have to be unique when everything lives in one folder, so the repo-engineering one is now called `untested-entry-points`. The installer still checks for collisions and prefixes a name with its plugin if one ever appears again.

The repository is MIT licensed, like the sources.

## Tell me what is wrong

If a skill gives you a wrong answer, misses something it should catch or claims more than it can show, I would like to know. Issues and pull requests are open on each source repository, and the [project list](/#projects) has them all. If you want a pack that does not exist yet, open an issue on [claude-skills](https://github.com/basitalisandhu/claude-skills) and say what job it should do.
